pts: E[Xₜ] = μ is constant over time.
Var(Xₜ) is finite and constant.
Cov(Xₜ, Xₜ₊ₕ) depends only on the lag h, not on t.
cards.pit: Strict stationarity is about all joint distributions; strict + finite second moments ⇒ weak, but weak ⇏ strict (except for Gaussian processes).

cards.q: What does the ACF tell you compared with the PACF?
pts: ACF ρ(h): correlation between Xₜ and Xₜ₋ₕ, including indirect effects through the lags in between.
PACF at lag h: correlation after removing the linear effect of lags 1, …, h − 1.
Identification: AR(p) ⇒ PACF cuts off after p; MA(q) ⇒ ACF cuts off after q.
cards.pit: In finite samples the cut-offs are noisy — combine with information criteria (AIC/BIC).

cards.q: What is the key distinction between AR(p) and MA(q)?
pts: AR(p): Xₜ = c + φ₁Xₜ₋₁ + … + φₚXₜ₋ₚ + εₜ — depends on past values of the series.
MA(q): Xₜ = μ + εₜ + θ₁εₜ₋₁ + … + θ_qεₜ₋q — depends on current and past shocks.
AR is stationary iff the roots of 1 − φ₁z − … − φₚzᵖ lie outside the unit circle; MA is always stationary, and invertible iff the roots of θ(z) lie outside it.
cards.pit: A stationary AR has an MA(∞) representation; an invertible MA has an AR(∞) representation.

pts: Each series is I(1): nonstationary with a unit root.
Some nontrivial linear combination βᵀXₜ is I(0), i.e. stationary.
It implies a long-run equilibrium and an error-correction model (VECM); it is the basis of pairs trading.
Tests: Engle–Granger (two-step), Johansen (multivariate).
cards.pit: Correlation ≠ cointegration: two series can have highly correlated returns and still drift apart in levels.

cards.q: Why can random train/test splitting be dangerous in time-series ML?
pts: A random split lets future information leak into training, so scores look too optimistic.
Use chronological / walk-forward (rolling-origin) evaluation.
With overlapping labels (e.g. 20-day forward returns), purge training samples whose label windows overlap the test set and add an embargo after it.
cards.pit: Scalers and feature selection must also be fit on the training window only.

pts: Conditional variance: hₜ = ω + α ε²ₜ₋₁ + β hₜ₋₁ with ω > 0, α, β ≥ 0.
It captures volatility clustering: a large shock raises next period’s variance.
α + β < 1 ⇒ covariance stationary with long-run variance ω / (1 − α − β); α + β near 1 means very persistent volatility.
cards.pit: Standard GARCH is symmetric; the leverage effect needs EGARCH or GJR-GARCH.

cards.q: What is the difference between white noise and a martingale difference sequence?
pts: White noise: zero mean, constant finite variance, zero autocorrelation at all nonzero lags.
MDS: E[εₜ | ℱₜ₋₁] = 0 — unpredictable in mean from the past.
An MDS with finite variance is uncorrelated; but white noise need not be an MDS (it can be nonlinearly predictable).
Example: ARCH errors are an MDS but not i.i.d. — returns unpredictable, volatility predictable.

cards.q: What is look-ahead bias in a trading backtest?
pts: The strategy uses information that was not available at the decision time.
Examples: revised macro data, restated fundamentals, trading at the same close used to compute the signal, today’s index constituents.
Fix: point-in-time data, align features by publication / availability timestamps, lag signals.
cards.pit: Using today’s index membership also creates survivorship bias.
